A [p-value](inference.qmd#def-p-value) answers a question about one hypothesis.
Many studies ask the question many times:
a gene expression study tests every gene for a difference between two tumor types,
and a screening study tests every candidate drug.
Each test that uses the usual [significance level](inference.qmd#def-significance-level)
has a small chance of flagging a null hypothesis that is true,
and those chances add up over thousands of tests.

This page does three things:

- shows how fast false positives accumulate;
- defines two error rates for a whole family of tests,
  the family-wise error rate and the false discovery rate;
- presents the standard procedures that control them:
  the Bonferroni correction, Holm's step-down procedure [@holm1979simple]
  and the Benjamini--Hochberg procedure [@benjamini1995controlling],
  with the adjusted p-values that report their results.

The next page, [permutation tests](permutation-tests.qmd),
shows how to compute a p-value without a distributional model.
These notes follow chapter 13 of @james2021islr2e.
